en: Had salt enough to sate a sheep.
She pulled them from his feet and flung them aside;
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Thus began her mischievous doings,
Making herself known as his sister,
And the rump-leather boots she had made
She put on Semetey.
Thereupon Kanykei,
Tormenting her heart in this way,
Without revealing herself as his mother,
Upon Semetey
Put the garments of a king.
His poor, fierce sister
Made herself known as his sister
And all the countless treasures
She put on Semetey.
The poor woman looking at him
Was sorely torn at heart.
When she looked at Semetey,
He seemed just like his father, Khan Manas.
Seeing this, Kanykei,
Without looking about her,
Without any thought for herself,
Resolved to give him the hidden
Gold left by the warrior.
From the little one left by her lord,
Your valiant mother Kanykei,
Once she set her mind, how could she hold back?
From the spring flowing from the valley,
She especially would not spare herself;
From the little one she had gained through mortal hardship,
The little one left by the winged steed,
Kanykei held nothing back,
From the little lamp left by the falcon.
Her many thoughts in turmoil,
She gazed at her son in grief.
'May I circle round you, little brother!
I mourn for the white palace,
My heart is full of grief;
Hear me, brother, without grieving.
A khan's doorway is Judgment Day:
One needs a way to step inside.
A king's doorway is solid iron:
One needs words to melt it.
Little brother, understand my conduct thus:
For a king to become a king,
Little brother, it takes a woman.
When black ice lay in great sheets,
When I, poor soul, was still a girl,
I grew headstrong in my courage;
Against your dear, wolf-maned brother-in-law,
I came up against him at fourteen.
I kept his court and gave him life;
Your brother-in-law, gone to the other world,
I made a khan renowned throughout the world.
I joined what had been severed;
From among the forty tribes
I gathered your brother-in-law's forty warriors.
I had him strike down every foe he met;
For your brother-in-law, gone to Judgment,
I had what he had lost gathered back again.
Your warrior brother-in-law was born in Altai;
When he reached the age of twelve,
He sought out and found Talas.
Let me tell of your brother-in-law Manas.
He was a lion blessed by Kyzyr;
All the mighty men gathered to him;
He was a warrior of surpassing fortune.
Your heroic brother-in-law, that outstanding one,
Was a warrior blessed by Baabedin.
All the champions united around him;
Such a mighty lion was he.
Among the infidels, that formidable one,
The Chinese Alooke in a distant land—
When he shattered that formidable foe
And drove him down toward Kashgar,
When he pursued Alooke and slew him,
When he had his fill of booty,
Leaving nothing untouched among twelve peoples,
Not even a horse-catching pole left to turn against him,
Manas rose as khan from among the Kyrgyz;
His very voice struck souls from bodies.
Of lands where his Akkula had not trodden,
Not one remained intact.
Of peoples who had not heard his battle cry,
Not one remained intact.
When he humbled Kokand,
When he laid waste to Margilan,
A black-spotted leopard
Raged at his flank,
Supporting him invisibly.
A star stirred in the sky;
He became a friend of a saint.
The stars of forty tribes stirred;
He became a friend of Kyzyr.
When Kyzyr blessed him abundantly,
Great Bakai, possessed of saintly power,
Became his friend for the hereafter,
Became his companion.
Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Taking a letter from the caliph,
Rode out in search of the blood-shedding hero;
Stirred by his own courage,
He met the warrior Manas.
Like stars in the sky,
They gathered as chosen companions;
They bound themselves for the other world.
Three mighty warriors came from three directions
And joined together.
When he journeyed to Mecca,
When he made his way into Medina,
From the desert of Mediyan
A hidden spring burst forth;
A voice sounded from the sky
And granted what he prayed for.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Naked, without trousers,
With a fair, wheat-colored face,
A gray-bearded dervish—
No dervish, but a saint—said:
'Youngest of the six lions,
You are my chosen one, Manas.
By the decree of God,
The elder Kaiyp has come before you;
I am your father Kaiyp.
I shall set your crooked ways straight;
My son, I shall support you in straits.
Among countless troops, I shall be your guiding sign;
If you travel alone, my foal,
I shall accompany you with a thousand troops.
I entrust you with one thing;
My chosen Manas, take it,
Fasten it firmly round your waist,
And campaign against the infidels.
For Islam, small as a palm,
For the few and varied Muslims,
Become a father.
The little band of Muslims,
When a dire, formidable foe comes,
Until you pass from this world,
Until your journey ends,
Keep them safe.
Gather those who are scattered,
If you desire a worthy faith.'
The Gray Pouch-Belt worn on campaigns,
When he fastened it at his waist with a cry,
Brought the Forty Chiltens as his companions;
When he fastened it at his waist with a shout,
Brought the White Ishan as his companion.
The Gray Pouch-Belt descended from heaven,
The belt that was a friend to his precious life,
He fastened at his waist with a cry;
When stubborn foes swarmed about him,
Your brother-in-law raised a shouting tumult.
I give you this as a gift;
My warrior brother, take it with you.
Saying, 'It was my valiant brother-in-law's,'
As a memento, little brother,
Fasten this round your waist as you go.
Saying, 'My sister is a widow,'
Remember now, my brother;
Do not dismiss him as gone to Judgment;
Keep your brother-in-law in mind.
Those who know call this
'The Gray Pouch-Belt descended from heaven.'
Those who do not know say,
'When he humbled Kokand,
When he sacked Margilan,
He took this belt by force.'
Would a blustering khoja
Possess a belt like this,
This Gray Pouch-Belt before us?
Can anyone prosper who says such things?
I give it as a memento; take it with you.
May I take your hardships upon myself;
Fasten it firmly round your waist.
My brother, come by from time to time;
Asking, 'How is she faring?'
Come and see your sister's face.'
Stepping softly, Kanykei
Now took the Gray Pouch-Belt in her hands.
To the little one she had gained through mortal hardship,
Entrusting him with the Gray Pouch-Belt,
She now fastened it snugly round his waist.
His majesty stood unshaken by any wind;
She longed to clasp her only one
To her breast, but could not.
Such was the Creator's torment,
The Almighty's overwhelming power.
She opened the door and led him out,
Managed to get him onto his horse,
Spoke softly, pouring out her feelings,
And pleaded, calling him 'little brother':
'Turn your horse's head a moment;
I shall tell you one more thing.
Stand a moment in the place ahead!
To the gated city of Bukhara
Go straight, my brother, without turning aside,
To your father Temir Khan's golden throne,
The royal plane-tree garden.
Without much talk, without a word,
Travel by day; do not journey by night.
Take Akbaran in your hand;
The Sarts playing the dutar—
Let them taste its thunder.
Ransack and plunder their possessions;
Of those wretches born for mischief,
Pull the goods out of their saddlebags.
Whoever talks back,
Offer him up as a sacrifice.
To those foul-hearted old wretches,
Give them a taste of sport.
Bear down upon their heads;
Scatter their four kinds of livestock;
Plunder their possessions;
Cause them thorough havoc.
Raid their mules and mares;
Bring back from them
Some of those far, far away.
If any of those villains comes near,
Strike his brains out.
Cause fierce havoc.
There are sixty mule-loads;
Their loads are cotton fiber.
Do as I say before you go;
To your sister, this bereaved, hapless woman,
Give them as a gift before you leave.
Alty-Shaar, Margilan,
Farther on Kokand and Samarkand,
Straight ahead Andijan,
The upper elder Ozubek,
The lower elder Kozubek,
Andijan's fork-bearded Synchybek,
And the Kushbegi of Kokand
Have pitched their tents;
With great komuzes whose bellies fill an armful,
They have had their dutars played,
Have boiled their pilaf thoroughly,
Have spread their food in abundance,
Have had their stallions grazed apart,
And some sixty of their Sarts
They have had sing their akush songs with vigor.
God must have bereft your father Temir Khan of sense;
All those Sarts
Must have asked for you as a hostage.
Your fool of a father, carried away with joy,
Must have said, "I shall give him."
With thirteen days between,
He must have made his promise.
Fixing their malice deliberately upon you,
They must have asked for you as a hostage.
If you go as a hostage, they will do you no good;
My brother, in the end they will not leave you unharmed.
They have prepared poison and salt;
They have a girl they have prepared as a sham.
They will play tricks and make you play;
